source_text: Sed quod meum est, inquit, fugio, ne peream, si negavero; illius est, si voluerit, etiam fugientem me reducere in medium. Hoc mihi prius responde: certus es te negaturum, si non fugeris, an incertus? Si enim certus, iam negasti, quia praesumendo te negaturum id despopondisti de quo praesumpsisti, et vane iam fugis, ne neges, qui, si negaturus es, iam negasti. Si vero incertus es, cur non ex aequalitate incerti metus inter utrumque eventum etiam confiteri te posse praesumis et salvum magis fieri, quo minus fugias, sicut negaturum te praesumis, ut fugias? Iam nunc aut in nobis est utrumque aut totum in deo. Si in nobis est confiteri aut negare, cur non id praesumimus, quod est melius, id est confessuros nos? Nisi si vis confiteri, pati non vis; nolle autem confiteri negare est. Si vero in deo totum est, cur non totum relinquimus arbitrio eius agnoscentes virtutem et potestatem, quod possit nos sicut fugientes reducere in medium, ita et non fugientes, immo et in medio populo conversantes obumbrare? Quale est, ut ad fugiendum deo honorem reddas, qui possit te etiam fugientem producere in medium, ad contestandum autem inhonores illum desperans potentiam protectionis ab illo? Quare non magis ex hac parte constantiae et fiduciae in deum dicis: Ego quod meum est facio; non discedo; deus, si voluerit, ipse me proteget? Hoc potius nostrum est, stare sub dei arbitrio, quam fugere sub nostre. Rutilius sanctissimus martyr, cum totiens fugisset persecutionem de loco in locum, etiam periculum, ut putabat, nummis redemisset, post totam securitatem, quam sibi prospexerat, ex inopinato apprehensus et praesidi oblatus tormentis dissipatus, credo pro fugae castigatione, dehinc ignibus datus passionem, quam vitarat, misericordiae dei retulit. Quid aliud voluit dominus nobis demonstrare hoc documento, quam fugiendum non esse, quia nihil fuga prosit, si deus nolit?
thought_title: The logic of flight and God's power
orientation: Tertullian is answering Fabius's opening objection that he flees to avoid denying, and now presses him with a dilemma about whether denial is certain or uncertain.
pass_a_gloss: But what is mine, he says, I flee, lest I perish, if I deny; it is his, if he wishes, to bring me back into the midst even fleeing. Answer me this first: are you certain that you will deny, if you do not flee, or uncertain? For if certain, you have already denied, because by presuming that you will deny you have pledged that about which you presumed, and in vain now you flee, lest you deny, you who, if you are going to deny, have already denied. But if you are uncertain, why do you not from the equality of uncertain fear between either outcome also presume that you can confess and rather be made safe, so that you flee less, just as you presume that you will deny, so that you flee? Now already either both are in us or the whole is in God. If it is in us to confess or to deny, why do we not presume that which is better, that is, that we will confess? Unless if you wish to confess, you do not wish to suffer; but to be unwilling to confess is to deny. But if the whole is in God, why do we not leave the whole to his judgment, recognizing the power and might, that he can bring us back into the midst just as fleeing, so also not fleeing, nay rather even shelter us while living in the midst of the people? What sort of thing is it, that for fleeing you give honor to God, who can bring you out into the midst even fleeing, but for bearing witness you dishonor him, despairing of the power of protection from him? Why do you not rather from this side of steadfastness and trust in God say: I do what is mine; I do not depart; God, if he wishes, will himself protect me? This is rather ours, to stand under God's judgment, than to flee under our own. Rutilius the most holy martyr, although he had so often fled persecution from place to place, and had even bought off the danger, as he thought, with coins, after all the security which he had foreseen for himself, unexpectedly seized and presented to the governor, torn apart by tortures, I believe for the chastisement of his flight, then given to the fires, he returned to the mercy of God the passion which he had avoided. What else did the Lord wish to show us by this example, than that one must not flee, because flight profits nothing, if God is unwilling?

choices.why: The verb despondeo means to promise or pledge formally; the perfect tense indicates a completed act of commitment, matching the argument that presumption is already denial.
Obumbro literally means to overshadow, but in this context of God's protection it conveys covering or sheltering from danger, which fits the contrast with being brought into the midst.
Contestor here refers to the act of confessing Christ before persecutors, which is the martyrdom sense in the brief; 'bearing witness' captures the public testimony aspect.
Nummus is a specific coin, and the plural here indicates money paid; 'coins' is concrete and matches the buying one's way out sense without using the banned 'bribe'.
Dissipo means to scatter or disperse, but with tortures it conveys physical destruction; 'torn apart' captures the violence of the martyrdom.
Documentum here means a lesson or proof by example; 'example' fits the rhetorical use of Rutilius as a demonstration.

pass_b_english: Someone objects, "But I am fleeing what belongs to me, so that I do not perish if I deny. It is God's part, if he wills, to bring me back into the midst even as I flee."

First answer me this: are you certain you will deny if you do not flee, or are you uncertain? If you are certain, you have already denied. By presuming you will deny, you have pledged the very thing you presumed, and now you flee in vain to avoid denying. If you are going to deny, you have already denied.

But if you are uncertain, why do you not, from the equal uncertainty of fear between the two outcomes, also presume that you can confess and be saved rather than flee, just as you presume you will deny so that you flee? At this point either both things are in our power or everything is in God's.
If confessing or denying is in our power, why do we not presume what is better, namely that we will confess? Unless you want to confess but do not want to suffer. And refusing to confess is denial.

But if everything is in God's power, why do we not leave everything to his judgment, recognizing his strength and power? Just as he can bring us back into the midst when we flee, so he can shelter us when we do not flee, and even when we are living among the people.

What kind of honor is it to give God credit for your flight, since he can bring you out into the midst even as you flee, but to dishonor him when it comes to bearing witness, despairing of the power of his protection? Why do you not rather say, from this side of steadfastness and trust in God: "I do what is mine to do; I do not leave; God himself will protect me if he wills"? This is more properly ours: to stand under God's judgment than to flee under our own.

Rutilius, that most holy martyr, had fled persecution from place to place so many times, and had even bought his way out of danger with coins, as he thought. After all the security he had arranged for himself, he was unexpectedly seized and handed over to the governor, torn apart by tortures, I believe as chastisement for his flight, and then given to the flames. And so he returned to God's mercy the suffering he had avoided.
What else did the Lord want to show us by this example than that we must not flee, because flight profits nothing if God is unwilling?
